verdict.probe_answer: Both arms' new tests reference the new rich_snapshot_frames/fold_or_typed_snapshot shape, which doesn't exist pre-change, so both fail to compile on old code (a real gate). Arm A: 2 new tests. rich_snapshot_folds_toolcall_interleaved drives the REAL store (record_event_sequenced, journal_fold_inputs, fold_journal_to_snapshot) end-to-end and asserts tool_call_id/title/tool_kind/status plus (seq,tag) — strongest test, validating the true pipeline not just the pure function. rich_snapshot_plan_latest_orphan_update_and_cursor is the standout: proves latest-Plan-wins, an orphan ToolCallUpdate (no base) framed at its own seq, AND cursor applied ONCE on the MERGED list (cursor=2 also drops the plan frame) — directly targets PFIX-H's riskiest edge. Arm B: 1 new test, hand-builds OrchEvent/TaskProgressSnapshot literals (bypassing the store) and only asserts status on the merged ToolCall frame plus tag order — its weakest/only test, since it never exercises Plan-latest, orphan-update, or cursor-on-rich-frames despite the task naming all three as required. Neither test is tautological, but Arm B's coverage is materially narrower — a cursor-before-merge bug would slip past Arm B's suite but be caught by Arm A's.
verdict.rationale: Both correctly restructure fold_or_typed_snapshot to return {snap, events} from one read, add rich_snapshot_frames merging node+rich frames with a single cursor-filter, swap both call sites, and preserve the sentinel/dedup_floor logic — functionally equivalent; no demonstrated (WRONG) bug in either. Arm A is more thorough: its second test proves cursor-on-merged and orphan/Plan-latest handling explicitly, its interleaved test round-trips through the real store, and it completes the task's explicit dead_code-removal step in reattach.rs (Arm B leaves stale #[allow(dead_code)] despite frame_from_orch now being used in server.rs). Arm A's fold also reuses the existing OrchEventKind enum directly rather than duplicating its field list into a new ToolCallFold struct with unreachable default fallbacks — slightly more DRY/maintainable. These are verifiable differences in test coverage and instruction compliance, not hypothetical risk.
